{{Short description|Statistical technique}}
{{Orphan|date=May 2023}}

{{Use dmy dates|date=February 2019}}
'''Commonality analysis''' is a statistical technique within [[multiple linear regression]] that decomposes a model's [[Coefficient of determination|''R''<sup>2</sup> statistic]] (i.e., explained variance) by all [[independent variable]]s on a [[dependent variable]] in a multiple linear regression model into commonality coefficients.<ref name="Nimon 2013">{{Cite journal|last1=Nimon|first1=Kim F.|last2=Oswald|first2=Frederick L.|date=October 2013|title=Understanding the Results of Multiple Linear Regression: Beyond Standardized Regression Coefficients|journal=Organizational Research Methods|volume=16|issue=4|pages=650–674|doi=10.1177/1094428113493929|issn=1094-4281|hdl=1911/71722|s2cid=55244970 |hdl-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Nimon|first1=Kim|last2=Reio|first2=Thomas G.|date=22 June 2011|title=Regression Commonality Analysis: A Technique for Quantitative Theory Building|journal=Human Resource Development Review|volume=10|issue=3|pages=329–340|doi=10.1177/1534484311411077|s2cid=144437265 |issn=1534-4843}}</ref> These coefficients are variance components that are uniquely explained by each independent variable (i.e., unique effects),{{#tag:ref|Commonality coefficients for the unique effects of the predictors are also known as ''uniqueness coefficients''.<ref name="Nimon 2013" /> The uniqueness coefficient of a given independent variable is equal to the square of the semipartial correlation of that independent variable with the dependent variable.<ref name="Nimon 2013" />|group="note"}} and variance components that are shared in each possible combination of the independent variables (i.e., common effects). These commonality coefficients sum up to the total variance explained (model ''R''<sup>2</sup>) of all the independent variables on the dependent variable. Commonality analysis produces {{math|2<sup>''k''</sup>&nbsp;−&nbsp;1}} commonality coefficients, where ''k'' is the number of the independent variables.

== Example ==
As an illustrative example, in the case of three independent variables (A, B, and C), commonality returns 7 ({{math|2<sup>3</sup>&nbsp;−&nbsp;1}}) coefficients: 
*The unique contributions of A, B, and C (three coefficients)
*The contribution common to each possible pair of variables (AB, BC, AC)
*The contribution common to all three variables (ABC)

The unique coefficient indicates to which degree the variable is independently associated with the dependent variable. Positive commonality coefficients indicate that a part of the explained variance of the dependent variable is shared between independent variables. Negative commonality coefficients indicate that there is a suppressor effects between independent variables.

== Calculation ==
The calculation of commonality coefficients can be done in principle with any software that calculates ''R''<sup>2</sup> (e.g., in [[SPSS]]; see Commonality Analysis: Demonstration of an SPSS
Solution for Regression Analysis<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ideals.illinois.edu/bitstream/handle/2142/15062/iSchoolCommonalityPosterFinal.pdf?|title=Commonality analysis: Demonstration of an SPSS solution for regression analysis|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190220181300/https://www.ideals.illinois.edu/bitstream/handle/2142/15062/iSchoolCommonalityPosterFinal.pdf|archive-date=February 20, 2019}}</ref>), however, this becomes quickly burdensome as number of independent variable increases. For example, with 10 independent variables, there are {{math|2<sup>10</sup>&nbsp;−&nbsp;1 {{=}} 1023}} commonality coefficients to be calculated. The yhat package<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Nimon|first1=Kim|last2=Lewis|first2=Mitzi|last3=Kane|first3=Richard|last4=Haynes|first4=R. Michael|date=May 2008|title=An R package to compute commonality coefficients in the multiple regression case: An introduction to the package and a practical example|journal=Behavior Research Methods|volume=40|issue=2|pages=457–466|doi=10.3758/BRM.40.2.457|pmid=18522056|issn=1554-351X|doi-access=free}}</ref> in [[R (programming language)|R]] can be used to calculate commonality coefficients, and to produce bootstrapped confidence intervals for commonality coefficients.
